articles.text: Col. Lounsberry, being interviewed in St. Paul, says that "of course" Gov. Pierce will be removed. In the face of the fact that Cleveland has said that there will be no removal, it looks as though Col. Lounsberry did not have a very high opinion of our President's veracity.
articles.summary: Packard mocks Col. Lounsberry's St. Paul claim that Governor Pierce will be removed despite Cleveland's statement to the contrary.

articles.text: A man named James Gray, living four miles north of Glenullen, was last week attacked by a couple of Indians, probably from the Fort Stevenson agency and nearly killed. He struggled desperately for his life in a hand to hand conflict with both of them and finally drove them off and it is thought killed one. There should be no delay in finding out who these Indians are and bringing them to justice. A case of this kind allowed to pass unpunished, may sow the seeds of many murders. Instant and condign punishment for misdeeds is the proper way, to discipline Indians as well as whites.
articles.summary: James Gray, living north of Glenullen, was attacked and nearly killed by two Indians last week; Packard demands they be brought to justice.

articles.text:
County Organization.

Again has this become a subject of paramount interest from the fact that the rate of taxation on the recent assessment of Billings county by Stark is now known and is either twelve or thirteen mills on the dollar. This is the rate on an assessed valuation in Billings county of over $500,000. It takes but little figuring to show that, should the amount of this assessment be paid to Stark county, it will be over $6,000, enough in itself almost to run a county organization in Billings county on a liberal scale.

We have before spoken of county organization as an economical plan for the county and it would be well to again bring it forward in that light.

First as to the officers. There will be needed a sheriff, justice of the peace, assessor, county attorney, three commissioners, treasurer and register of deeds. All county business can be transacted by this number of officers as well as by a greater number.

Besides officers, the running expenses of the county are included in buildings, school and a few other expenses which are trifling. The whole will amount to about $1,200 a year.

The shersff's office will cost more than any other but ought not to go over $600 or $800 a year. Sheriff Sebastian of Stark county, says that his office will cost this year about $2,000. This probably includes five times the mileage and fees that a sheriff here will have, as Mr. Sebastian has made numerous trips into counties attached to Stark Co. which our Sheriff will not need to do. $600 should be abundant for this office. A justice of the peace will not cost over $100 a year, the assessor $100, the county attorney $150; three commissioners each, $150. $450; register of deeds, $150. The treasurer gets a certain per cent. for handling the county money, but nothing as a salary. His per cent. will probably amount to about $300. This makes a total for salaries of about $1,850 per year. To be on the safe side, call it $2,500, add the $1,500 for sundries and we have as an outside, $4,000 for the ordinary running expenses of the county.

And now, what resources have we to meet these expenses? In the first place, there is the railroad tax. With a mileage of twenty-four miles, it was estimated by County Attorney Long of Mandan, that we would receive $3,400. Since then our limits have been stretched so that we have thirty-six miles of rail-road with a consequent tax of over $5,000.

In addition to the rail-road tax, we have the liquor license, which is now $1,200. This amount, Morton county now receives, but of course it will stay in Billings county after organization.

This makes a total of $6,200 to pay the ordinary running expenses and not a cent raised by taxation.

The first year there will be extra expenses, such as books, safes etc., but scarcely enough to make up the difference between the running expenses and the $6,200.

Suppose now, we add the $6,000 which must certainly be paid to Stark county unless we organize soon and which of itself would be enough to pay the running expenses of the county. It will be raised on an assessment of $500,000, which with our increased boundaries and former undervaluation could easily be raised to $750,000 or more. This will almost all be a surplus and will erect good county buildings, grade roads, build bridges and then leave a handsome sum in the treasury.

In view of the above facts, the matter of organization is being seriously considered by the stockmen, as it cannot but result in good to all.

No definite action has as yet been taken in respect to county officers. but the names most prominently mentioned are J. L. Truscott, Jos. A. Ferris and Mr. Rowe of Rowe, Parker & Easton for commissioners, Fred Willard for sheriff, Wm. VanDriesche for treausurer and "Judge" Gordon for justice of the peace. The choice for commissioners would of course have been different but that our county has been enlarged by the changing of the territorial lines and it is thought best to give Beaver creek a representation. Of course all the names mentioned are subject to approval and we merely voice the common sentiment in mentioning them. They are all good men however, in whose hands no one will fear to entrust the welfare of the county and are every man of them above any suspicion of dishonesty.
articles.summary: Packard argues that organizing Billings County would pay for itself from railroad tax and liquor licenses rather than paying some $6,000 in taxes to Stark County, and lists the men most mentioned for county offices.

articles.summary: J. A. VanEeghen has been west seeking horses to stock his Garner creek range next spring.

articles.text: The worst black eye the cattle market has had this season, was received last week in Chicago. Native shipping and dressed beef cattle dropped 40@70c. and most grades of western cattle, 50@75c. The highest price received for Montana rangers during the week, was $4.15 and some scalawag cows sold at $1.00. Texas cattle about held their own. The receipts in Chicago last week were 45,500 as against 48,000 the week before. Foreign markets were weak and lower and exporters did but little business. The prices were a little steadier at the close of the week.
articles.summary: Chicago cattle prices fell sharply last week, the worst drop of the season.

articles.text: A case will come off in Dickinson tomorrow, that will be extremely interesting as involving a test case which it is for the interest of every stockman on the river to have decided; although there are none but will regret to see the case assume such prominence. It seems that during the progress of the round-up, an animal was found that besides a blotched brand, had also one of the brands of the Bad Lands Cattle Co. This brand was vinted by the round-up and the animal sold as a maverick. For this reason, suit has been brought for grand larceny. The case has an unfortunate side, as no one can believe that there was any intention of stealing on the part of any members while no one can blame Mr. Wadsworth for wanting to clear himself of the suspicion of having branded some other man's animal. It would probably have been better to have settled the matter by arbitration; but the law must now take its course.
articles.summary: A grand larceny test case over an animal bearing a Bad Lands Cattle Co. brand that the round-up vented and sold as a maverick is to be heard in Dickinson tomorrow.

articles.text: The round-up came in to Medora Saturday and ended the work by rounding-up Andrew's creek on Sunday. Taking everything into consideration, the work was done as thoroughly as possible. The principal cause of complaint is that cattle were missed and that there will be an undue amount of mavericks in the spring. How true these reports are, only time will tell. There is no one who says that anyone shirked his duty. On the other hand, as all concur that every man worked hard, we are brought to the facts in the case: there were not enough men on the round-up. The complaint of a year ago last spring, that the riders were not well enough mounted, has almost disappeared. The complaint of too few men is as serious as that of too few or too poor horses and should be remedied as quickly. Round-up work is no "soft snap" and twenty-five men cannot do forty men's work any more than the best kind of a cow-boy, with a string of four or five poor horses can do one man's work. This is a matter that should be attended to at the next meeting of the association. The round-up lasted twenty-seven days and worked the Little Missouri and tributaries from below the mouth of Big Beaver on the north to the mouth of Little Beaver on the south and also the Big Beaver and its tributaries.
articles.summary: The fall round-up came in to Medora Saturday and finished on Andrew's creek Sunday after twenty-seven days; Packard says it was short of men.

articles.text: Herbert D. Hostetter of Pittsburgh, who has been visiting Howard Eaton for some time, accidentally cut himself in the foot a few days ago and is now in Glendive, under the care of Dr. Duncan. The hurt is not serious but will lay up the patient for some days.
articles.summary: Herbert D. Hostetter, visiting Howard Eaton, cut his foot and is under a doctor's care in Glendive.

articles.text: John Munro has decided to again embark in the sheep business, this time on his own account. His ranch will probably be in the neighborhood of Mingusville. We wish Johnny only the best of success, but are sorry that the history of the sheep business in this country doesn't hold forth very bright promises for the future.
articles.summary: John Munro will start a sheep ranch near Mingusville.

articles.text: As the shooting contests of the Gun club were still unfinished and Seth Wyland, who was at the head of those who had completed their scores, started for a winter's hunting trip Monday, it was deemed best to give him the first prize. There were two contestants who had not finished their scores and who stood good chances of winning but as there had been too long a delay it was deemed the fair thing to make the above decision.
articles.summary: The Gun club awarded first prize to Seth Wyland, who left Monday on a winter hunting trip.

articles.text: The Marquise is especially interested in having a school started here and has renewed her proposal to pay the teacher. The room recently vacated by Roberts & Co. will make a first-rate school-room. Nothing but a little effort on the part of the school board is now required to set things going. Several persons have objected, thinking it was the intention to start a Catholic school. We are assured that no such intention exists.
articles.summary: The Marquise de Morès renewed her offer to pay a teacher for a Medora school; the old Roberts & Co. room is proposed as the schoolroom.

articles.text: It is a good time now to mention that the petty thieving which has been going on whenever occasion offered, must come to a stop at once. There are at least two persons here who are known to possess this rustling spirit and who will be cinched to the limit the first time after this fair warning that they are caught stealing the value of a pin. A word to the wise is sufficient and ought to work on rustlers.
articles.summary: The paper warns that petty thieving in Medora must stop.

articles.text: It is time that the new school board took action on the subject of holding a school this winter. The Marquise has already offered to pay the teacher's salary, an offer that may be withdrawn if some steps are not taken soon by the school board. There is no reason why the children here should not have as good educational facilities as is needed. The remaining expenses, beside the teacher, are trifling and could readily be raised by subscription. Brace up, honorable members of the school board!
articles.summary: The paper urges the new school board to act on the Marquise's offer to pay a teacher.

articles.headline: In Memoriam
articles.text:
In Memoriam.

DIED—Sunday morning, Oct. 25, of concussion of the brain, J. Hayes Moore.

The above notice comes like a shock to everyone in the Bad Lands. Hayes Moore was well known and liked here as a quiet, unassuming man who would go far out of his way to help anyone and who never had an enemy.

He was born in Steubenville, Ohio, the eldest son of Geo. D. and Lydia A. Moore and at the time of his death was thirty-eight years old. He came to this place in 1879 as clerk for his brother Frank, who at that time was sutler at the Cantonment. For the last two years he has been at the KC ranch on Garner creek.

The accident which caused his death occurred last Thursday at the mouth of Garner creek. He had gone on horseback to watch the progress of the round-up and having to move a little to avoid a herd of cattle, his horse stumbled and fell and in rolling over, struck Hayes just above the temple, knocking him insensible. He remained constantly in this state up to the time of his death, which occurred at 4:30 Sunday morning. The funeral took place Tuesday at twelve o'clock at the KC ranch. D. K. Wade officiated by reading the burial service and the remains were borne to their last resting-place on the summit of the high butte back of the ranch by the pall-bearers Messrs. Merrifield, Ferris, Myers, Bennett, Willis Eaton, Truscott, Elliott and Rowe.
articles.summary: Obituary of J. Hayes Moore of the KC ranch, fatally injured when his horse fell during the round-up at the mouth of Garner creek.

articles.text: The Marquise and hunting party returned from their hunt Monday. They had good success.

articles.text: Jos. Ferris started for St. Paul yesterday morning to lay in his winter stock of goods. He will be gone about a week.

articles.summary: Johnny Sawyer dislocated his shoulder Saturday night; Dr. Robarts set it.

articles.text: Before the winter's snows have whitened the ground very long, there will be at least two more marriages to record, or the Cow Boy is greatly mistaken.
articles.summary: The paper predicts at least two more marriages before long.

articles.text: J. H. Gilmore of Minneapolis, one of the owners of the "square 47" outfit, was in Medora Saturday, and left his brand, which will appear in the next issue of the Cow Boy.
articles.summary: J. H. Gilmore of the "square 47" outfit visited Medora and left his brand for publication.

articles.text: The new stock-yards were broken in Saturday, by the shipment of three cars of cattle, two of 76 (monogram) bar and one of quarter circle diamond. Alden Eaton and Will Dantz accompanied them and will sell them in St. Paul, where small lots can be sold to better advantage than in Chicago.
articles.summary: The new Medora stock-yards were first used Saturday to ship three cars of cattle to St. Paul.

articles.text: Sheriff Sebastian of Dickinson, dropped into the Cow Boy office Tuesday, while in Medora on business. He has just returned from Canada on a successful search after the stock stolen from the Gallien Bros., at Belfield last summer. They had been confiscated from Wm. Roberts and Tommy Hughes as smuggled property and sold by the Canadian government. Roberts and Hughes were convicted of smuggling and each served six months in prison. After the usual red-tape delay, the proceeds of the government sale will be turned over to the Gallien Bros.
articles.summary: Sheriff Sebastian, back from Canada, reported recovering the value of stock stolen from the Gallien Bros. at Belfield.
